title: Estimating the Value of a New Transit Option
research_question: What is the effect of introducing a new urban rail transit line on residential and commercial property values in the surrounding neighborhoods, and how do these neighborhood-level effects compare to localized price gradient effects based on proximity to transit stations? Does new rail transit function primarily as a transportation amenity capitalized through access, or as a driver of broader neighborhood economic development?
data_description: The study uses parcel-level administrative records from the Mecklenburg County (North Carolina) assessor's office covering all single-family homes, condominiums, and commercial properties in the City of Charlotte. The dataset includes structural characteristics (e.g., square footage, bathrooms, bedrooms, age, lot size, 55 building attributes), geographic coordinates of parcels, and complete sales transaction histories from 1994 through June 2008 (58 quarterly periods). Constructed variables include Euclidean distance from each parcel to the nearest actual or proposed rail transit station, distance to the central business district, and distance to nearby interstates. Neighborhood-level covariates come from the City of Charlotte's 2000 Neighborhood Quality of Life Study, based on Neighborhood Statistical Areas, including population density, income, ownership rates, school outcomes, bus access, and property/violent crime indices. Final samples include roughly 151,896 single-family sales, 37,429 condominium sales, and 4,352 commercial sales.
institutional_context: Charlotte, North Carolina began planning a light rail transit (LRT) system in the late 1980s. In 1994 the City adopted a land-use plan targeting five transit corridors radiating from downtown, and in November 1998 county voters approved a half-cent sales tax to fund transit. After an extended planning process that evaluated three finalist corridors—South, Northeast, and Southeast—the Metropolitan Transit Commission officially selected the South corridor in September 2000 as the first LRT alignment. The 9.6-mile South Line, with 15 stations and a total cost exceeding $450 million, opened for service in November 2007. The Northeast and Southeast corridors were considered throughout the planning process but were not chosen for the initial build-out, although potential station locations along these alignments were later identified for possible future extensions. This planning history creates comparable corridors that were considered for, but did not receive, rail transit during the sample period.
